name: Narasimhaswamy Temple, Namakkal
significance: A cave temple cut into the rock below Namakkal Fort, enshrining a seated Narasimha with his consort Namagiri Tayar. Its panels of Trivikrama, Narasimha slaying Hiranyakashipu and the reclining Vishnu make it an important example of early South Indian rock-cut sculpture.
story: Lakshmi is said to have performed penance here after Narasimha refused to forgive Hiranyakashipu; the shaligrama image Hanuman carried for her grew into the hill on which Narasimha then made his abode.

name: Thirukondeeswaram Pasupatheeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Tiruvarur district counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines praised in the Tamil Saiva canon. It was sung by the Nayanar saint Tirunavukkarasar (Appar) in his Tevaram hymns.

name: Thiruvallam Sree Parasurama Temple
significance: Standing on the bank of the Karamana River, this is the only Kerala temple with Parasurama as the presiding deity and is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams. It is a protected monument of the Kerala Department of Archaeology and carries sub-shrines for Brahma, Matsya, Murugan, Veda Vyasa, Ayyappa, Krishna and Ganesha.
story: Parasurama is said to have raised Kerala from the sea with his axe and then called on the serpent king Vasuki to sweeten the salt-laden soil, after which serpents became guardians of the land.

name: Thrissilery Shiva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Wayanad attributed to the Chera kings and reckoned about a thousand years old. It is ritually bound to the nearby Thirunelly Vishnu Temple: ancestral rites performed at Thirunelly are held to be incomplete until the pilgrim also visits here.
story: The separate Jala Durga shrine within the compound is said to have been consecrated by the sage Parashurama.

name: Punnainallur Kothandaramar Temple
deity: Rama as Kothandaramar (with Sita and Lakshmana)
significance: An 18th-century Rama temple near Thanjavur, one of the 88 shrines of the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam administered by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE department. It preserves shaligrama sculptures presented to the ruler of Thanjavur by a king of Nepal, and its walls carry painted episodes from the Ramayana.

name: Trithala Maha Siva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the southern bank of the Bharathappuzha, probably raised in the 9th–10th centuries and noted for marking the transition from Chola to Pandya temple architecture. It is one of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and its lingam, formed of river sand, is never anointed.
story: Agnihotri, eldest of the twelve children of Vararuchi in the Parayi petta panthirukulam legend, is said to have heaped river sand into a mound that hardened into a Shiva lingam when his mother tried to remove it.

name: Nalpathaneeswaram Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in Alappuzha district reckoned the forty-eighth foundation of the sage Khara, who is also credited with the Ettumanur and Kaduthuruthi temples. It remains one of the oldest Kerala temples still run under a Raja Sasana copper-plate grant, administered by the Kozhisseril, Payippattu and Mullakkeril Kaimal families.
story: The locality was once called Pandavar Veli, and four large stones a kilometre east of the temple are held to have been used by the Pandavas to heat milk during their exile.

name: Tiruppaatrurai Adhimooleswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple carrying several Chola-period inscriptions and counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam, praised by the 7th-century Nayanar saint Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram. It is run by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Board and keeps six daily rituals and three annual festivals.
story: A Chola king hunting here loosed an arrow at a bird and struck an anthill that began to ooze milk; Shiva then appeared in his dream to reveal his presence, and the king built the temple on the spot.

name: Thrikkadavoor Sree Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, situated in Kollam district and administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board. It is known for its golden flagstaff and a ten-day Srattu festival held in the Malayalam month of Kumbham.
story: The sage Mrikandu and his wife Marudmati are said to have obtained the short-lived son Markandeya here; when Yama cast his noose it fell instead around the lingam, and Shiva overcame him and granted the boy deathlessness.

name: Nalukulangara Maha Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Kuthiathode panchayat, Alappuzha district, whose presiding Bhadrakali is known locally as Nalukulangara Amma. Its outer shrines carry Shiva, Murugan and Saraswati.

name: Padanilam Parabrahma Temple
significance: An unusual Kerala shrine with no enclosing wall or roof and no conventional idol, where a stone Om symbol beneath open tree cover is worshipped as Parabrahma. It was one of the major temples of the former Travancore state and served as the administrative centre of the Nooranad region.
story: The name Padanilam is traced to pada, battle, after the fighting between local chieftains over control of the temple and its villages, which is said to have ended when Pazhoor Panamana Thampuran intervened by fasting.

name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Cheyyar
significance: A Shiva temple at Thiruvadhipuram in Cheyyar, formerly known as Thiruvothur, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Tamil Saiva canon. Tradition at the site records the saint Tirugnanasambandar turning a male palm tree into a female one, and Arunagirinathar worshipping Murugan here.
story: When Sambandar could not tell this temple apart from the neighbouring Devadi Raja Perumal temple, Ganesha is said to have appeared before him and pointed out the Shiva shrine.

name: Thirumangalam Sree Maha Vishnu Siva Temple
significance: A temple at Engandiyur in Thrissur district housing Maha Vishnu and Shiva in separate east-facing sanctums. It is one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala and is managed by the Kattumadam Devaswam Trust.
story: The Shiva lingam is held to be swayambhu, self-manifested, and installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Thiruvatta Mahadeva Temple
significance: One of the earliest temples in Kerala and among its 108 famous Shiva shrines, built under the Kulasekhara Perumals of the second Chera dynasty. The Vazhappally copper-plate inscription issued in the reign of the Chera king Rama Rajasekhara refers to this Shiva temple.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva idol here in the Treta Yuga.

name: Anthikad Karthyayani Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Anthikad in Thrissur district, counted among the 108 Durga temples of Kerala. It is administered by the Cochin Devaswom Board.

name: Padayanivettom Devi Temple
significance: A twin-goddess temple at Vallikunnam in Mavelikkara taluk, which records indicate has stood for at least 1,200 years. It preserved older ritual forms of worship such as Padayani, Thottam pattu and Kalamezhuthu pattu, and a Devaprashna inquiry confirmed the presence of its two goddesses.
story: The place is said to be named for a Padayani performance during which villagers glimpsed two radiant women by torchlight, taken to be the two goddesses, for whom temples were then founded.

name: Tirukkandalam Sivanandeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tirukkandalam, formerly Tirukkallil, in Tiruvallur district, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams. It was sung by the Nayanar saint Sambandar in the early medieval Tevaram hymns.

name: Tiruchopuram Mangalapureeswarar Temple
significance: A coastal Shiva temple in Cuddalore district, one of the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams glorified in the early medieval Tevaram. Its hymns are attributed to the Nayanar saint Sambandar.

name: Nadapuram Iringannur Siva Temple
significance: One of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala and among the oldest in Kozhikode district, with a two-tiered rectangular tiled sanctum. It is reckoned one of the three Thrikkapaleeswaram shrines of that list.
story: Tradition credits the sage Parashurama with installing the idol, and the village name Iringannur is explained as 'place of the two-eyed one' from the deity's distinctive two-eyed Sadashiva form.

name: Kasi Viswanathar Temple, Tenkasi
significance: Founded in the 13th century by the Pandya ruler Parakrama Pandyan and enlarged by the Madurai Nayaks from the 16th century, this granite-walled complex gives Tenkasi its name as the 'Kasi of the south'. Inscriptions of 1384 record grants of houses and villages to Brahmins for Vedic recitation, and its long-flat tower was rebuilt as a 180-foot seven-tiered gopuram completed in 1990.
story: Shiva is said to have appeared to the king in a dream and told him to follow a column of ants; the temple was raised where the trail ended, sparing his people the journey to Varanasi.

name: Thrippalur Mahadeva Temple
significance: A temple on the bank of the Gayatri river at Alathur, one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala, with three shrines: square sanctums for Shiva and Krishna and a circular one for Narasimha. It was once held by the Kavalappara Swarupam of the Palakkad rulers and is referred to in several Malayalam classics.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama installed the Shiva idol in the Treta Yuga, the temple being raised to calm the god's power.

name: Thiruvambadi Sri Krishna Temple
significance: A Thrissur city temple where Krishna in child form and Bhadrakali are worshipped with equal standing, with sub-shrines for Ganesha, Sastha and Brahmarakshasa. It leads one of the two rival contingents of the annual Thrissur Pooram festival.
story: The goddess here is regarded as the younger sister of the Bhagavathi of the Paramekkavu temple, the Pooram's other contingent.

name: Paippad Puthenkavu Bhagavathi Temple
significance: An old Bhagavathi shrine on the Changanassery–Kaviyoor road about five kilometres from Changanassery. It is run by an elected Devaswom board drawn from two NSS Karayogams, and its annual festival falls on the Bharani day of the Malayalam month of Meenam.

name: Sivalokanathar Temple, Gramam
significance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam in Viluppuram district whose original Chola complex was rebuilt in masonry by Vijayanagara kings in the 16th century. It was converted into a stone temple under Parantaka I around 940 CE and carries inscriptions of the medieval Cholas, the Pandyas and the Rashtrakutas.
story: Local legend explains the older name Thirumundeeswaram from the gatekeepers Thindi and Mundi who worshipped Shiva here; another account has King Chokkalingam find a lingam beneath a lotus while hunting and raise the temple over it.

name: Annappanpettai Sundareswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Sirkazhi block of Mayiladuthurai district, at a place historically called Kalikamoor, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams. It was sung by Tirugnanasambandar in the Tevaram, and the sage Parasara is held to have worshipped here.

name: Mallinathaswamy Jain Temple, Mannargudi
significance: One of the best known of the old Jain tirthas of Tamil Nadu, raised at Mannargudi under Chola rule in the 12th century. It has a three-tiered rajagopura, a two-tiered vimana and a mahamandapa built in Maratha style; the present 56 cm image of the presiding Tirthankara was made in 1986.

name: Shri Vishwanath Mandir, BHU
significance: Planned by Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya and funded by the Birla family, this marble temple on the Banaras Hindu University campus took from 1931 to 1966 to build and is modelled on the Kashi Vishwanath temple. Its shikhara rises about 77 m, nine shrines are gathered into one structure, and the full text of the Bhagavad Gita is inscribed on its inner walls.

name: Chennakeshava Temple, Hullekere
significance: A soapstone ekakuta shrine built in 1163 CE by a minister of the Hoysala king Narasimha I, with lathe-turned pillars, tiers of miniature vimanas and the Hoysala royal emblem on its sukhanasi. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: The emblem carried on the tower shows Sala, the legendary founder of the Hoysala line, stabbing a lion.

name: Mrityunjay Mahadev Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple at Daranagar in Varanasi whose present building dates to the 18th century, though the smaller shrines it contains are held to be far older. It is the principal place in the city for the recitation of the Mrityunjaya mantra, and its compound holds a celebrated well.
story: Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods, is said to have emptied all his medicines into the temple well, so that its water heals illness and guards devotees against untimely death.

name: Bhavanarayana Temple, Bapatla
builtDisplay: 15th c.; foundation credited to Kubja Vishnuvardhana
significance: The temple that gives Bapatla its name, whose foundation the article credits to the Vengi Chalukya ruler Kubja Vishnuvardhana, who took the title Paramabhagavata for it. It is a centrally protected monument of national importance and carries inscriptions in Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit.

name: Thalassery Jagannatha Temple
significance: Consecrated by the social reformer Sree Narayana Guru in 1908 at the invitation of Varathoor Kaniyil Kunhikannan of Thalassery, this shrine became a landmark of the movement to open temple worship to the Thiyya community. A statue of the Guru was added to the compound in 1927.
story: The Guru is said to have seen his own statue at Colombo while it was still in transit from Italy to the temple.

name: Baba Garib Sthan Mandir (Garibnath Temple)
significance: The principal Shiva temple of Muzaffarpur, popularly called the Deoghar of Bihar for the crowds it draws during Shravan. Its lingam is said to have come to light when a stand of peepal trees on the site was felled.
story: When the trees were cut a blood-red substance is said to have flowed from them, a great lingam was uncovered, and Baba appeared in the landowner's dream directing that worship continue there.

name: Anandavalleeswaram Temple, Kollam
deity: Shiva as Ananda Swaroopan (with Parvati as Anandavally)
significance: An 11th-century temple in Kollam city, one of the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala, whose teak sanctum is reckoned some 1,200 years old. The article notes it as the only Indian temple to hold Krishna, Maha Vishnu, Bhoomi Devi and Lakshmi Devi consecrated together under one roof.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the Shiva idol, and the name is explained from anandam, joy, the state in which god and goddess are held to dwell here.

name: Vahisvaramudayar Temple, Malayadipatti
significance: A rock-cut cave shrine at Malayadipatti in Kulathur taluk, attributed to Kuvaavan Satthan around 730 CE and carrying an inscription of the Pallava king Nandivarman (775–826 CE). It is one of a twin pair of cave temples at the site, the other dedicated to Vishnu.

name: Panayur Palur Shiva Temple
significance: One of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, standing near Vaniyamkulam in Palakkad district. Its east-facing square sanctum is built in the kukkudakruthi form, and Maha Shivaratri is its principal festival.
story: Folklore counts it among the shrines whose idol was installed by the sage Parashurama.

name: Anjumoorthy Temple
significance: A temple at Anjumoorthy Mangalam in Palakkad district whose presiding deity is Sudarshana, set in a compound of five structures. Its age is given inconsistently in the sources, from about five hundred to about fifteen hundred years.

name: Tirunettur Mahadeva Temple
deity: Shiva as Sri Parameswara (with Maha Vishnu as Vaikundeswara)
significance: A 5.5-acre temple compound at Vyttila in Ernakulam district holding separate east-facing Shiva and Vishnu shrines. It is reckoned one of the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala, and the Vishnu shrine is said to have been added at the suggestion of Vilwamangalam Swamiyar.
story: The Shiva shrine is counted among the 108 that the sage Parashurama is held to have established across Kerala.

name: Pamani Naganathar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Pamani, historically Tiru Padaleswaram, counted among the 275 Paadal Petra Sthalams and sung by Sambandar, Sundarar and Appar in the Tevaram. It serves as a Rahu–Ketu parihara sthalam, with its remedial rites performed on Fridays and Sundays.

name: Kanjilassery Maha Siva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple at Chemancheri in Kozhikode district, counted among the 108 Shiva temples of Kerala and also housing Maha Vishnu.
story: Tradition holds that the sage Parashurama installed the idol, and that Kasi, Kanchipuram, Kanjirangad and Kanjilassery were all founded at the same moment.

name: Kalayat Ancient Bricks Temple Complex
significance: An 8th-century group of red-brick shrines at Kalayat in Kaithal district, laid out as a panchayatana of five temples of which two survive. They are built of locally made bricks laid without mortar or plaster, the Shiva shrine following the pancharatha plan and its shikhara bricks forming a beehive pattern.
story: The place name is traced to Kapilayatana, the abode of the sage Kapila, and the temples are popularly attributed to Raja Salban (Shalivahana).

name: Pananchery Mudikkode Shiva Temple
significance: A west-facing Shiva temple at Mudikkode in Pananchery, about 12 km from Thrissur, counted among the 108 famous Shiva temples of Kerala. Maha Shivaratri in the month of Kumbham is its main festival.
story: Folklore credits the sage Parashurama with installing the idol.

name: Dharmesvara Temple, Kondrahalli
significance: A Shiva temple at Kondrahalli in Hoskote taluk dated to 1065 CE and built in the Chola period. Its temple tank is tied to the Mahabharata, and the site is discussed in the literature on Indian temple architecture.
story: The tank here is held to be where the Yaksha Prashna took place: four Pandava brothers fell dead at its water, and Dharmaraja answered the Yaksha's questions to win their lives back from Yama.

name: Manakkattu Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple at Pallippad in Karthikappalli taluk, administered through four NSS Karayogams. Kunjekutty Pilla, known as Valyachan and an army chief under Dharma Raja Karthika Thirunal Rama Varma of Travancore, is remembered as its foremost devotee.
story: The idol is said to have been found when a farming woman struck a stone with her curved knife and it bled, centuries after the local shrines burned in the fire Arjuna set to the Khandava forest at Krishna's bidding.

name: Deepanayakaswamy Jain Temple, Deepangudi
significance: A Jain temple at Deepangudi in Tiruvarur district with a three-tiered stucco-figured rajagopura, a vimana on an upapeeta and peeta, and front, artha and maha mandapas. The village takes its name from the presiding Tirthankara, and an inscription of Rajendra Chola II uncovered in 2009 records a donation by a Jain named Nandhian.
